Accordingly, ⟦Luke 4:21|Luke 4:21⟧ may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea

In some languages it may be necessary to construct a descriptive equivalent for ‘sandbank,’ for example, ‘a hill of sand just beneath the surface of the water’ or ‘a ridge of sand hidden by the water.’

For example, in the first part of ⟦Revelation 18:7|Revelation 18:7⟧ one may translate in some languages ‘she honored herself very much and lived in great luxury, and so give her very much suffering and grief.’ In the case of ⟦Hebrews 1:4|Hebrews 1:4⟧, one may translate ‘God gave his Son a name that was more important than the name of the angels; therefore, God’s Son is greater than the angels.’

s.c: τράχηλος also occurs in the NT in certain idiomatic expressions, for example, ‘to fall on the neck of someone’ (⟦Luke 15:20|Luke 15:20⟧ and ⟦Acts 20:37|Acts 20:37⟧) in the sense of ‘to embrace’ (LN 34.64), and ‘to put down their necks’ (⟦Romans 16:4|Romans 16:4⟧) meaning ‘to risk their lives’ (LN 21.8). It is rare indeed that one can translate such idioms literally, since ‘to fall on the neck of someone’ may readily suggest a murderous attack, and ‘to risk one’s neck’ may be simply meaningless, since the custom of beheading as a means of execution may be relatively unknown.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: to have such awe or respect for a person as to involve a measure of fear
s.g: to fear; to show great reverence for; to show great respect for
s.c: In a number of languages there are serious problems involved in speaking of ‘fearing God,’ for this might imply merely ‘to be scared of God’ as though God were some kind of bogeyman. If there is a term with the meaning of ‘awe’ (perhaps in a phrase such as ‘to stand in awe of’), this may be an adequate equivalent. In some instances awe is expressed idiomatically as ‘to stand with one’s heart in one’s throat’ or ‘to be in someone’s presence with one’s heart beating fast.’|For another interpretation of τρέμω in ⟦2 Peter 2:10|2 Peter 2:10⟧, see LN 25.259.

For example, ‘a third of the trees’ would be rendered as ‘every third tree,’ and ‘a third of the earth was consumed by fire’ would be rendered as ‘the third part of the earth was consumed by fire’ or ‘having divided the earth into three parts, one part was destroyed by fire.’

s.dp: Non-Linear Movement

s.c: It is difficult to know precisely the significance of the phrase τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα. It probably had a technical sense which has been lost, but clearly it is parallel in meaning to παραλλαγή ‘change, alteration’ (LN 58.44). In some languages it may be best to translate this expression in ⟦James 1:17|James 1:17⟧ as ‘in whom there is no change or variation.’

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
s.c: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as ⟦Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11⟧ as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of τροχός ‘wheel,’ not occurring in the NT) a period of time of indefinite length, characterized by recurring events or patterns
s.c: In some languages τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως may be best rendered as ‘the very way in which we live’ or ‘the manner of our life.’ For another interpretation of τροχός in ⟦James 3:6|James 3:6⟧, see LN 61.5.

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: a relatively deep concave dish used for holding or cooking food or liquids; usually made of clay, but also metals
s.c: In the two NT occurrences (⟦Matthew 26:23|Matthew 26:23⟧; ⟦Mark 14:20|Mark 14:20⟧) τρύβλιον can be understood as a part of an idiom (literally ‘to dip one’s hands into the bowl with someone’) meaning ‘to share a meal with someone.’ If, however, the idiom is to be translated literally (and this is normally the case), there are certain difficulties involved, since a literal rendering of ‘to dip one’s hand into a bowl’ might mean literally putting one’s fingers or hand into a bowl rather than dipping in food which one holds in the hand. An idiomatic interpretation of ‘sharing a meal with someone’ or ‘eating together with’ may be preferable. But if one does translate the idiom somewhat literally, it is important in some languages to render this phrase as ‘to dip food into a bowl together with someone’ or ‘to jointly dip food into sauce.’

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: to pick or gather ripe fruit (especially used of grapes){N:001}

s.dp: Animals › Birds
s.d: Asiatic Rock dove: bird with a blue-gray color with a pinkish sheen to the neck feathers and a black tip on its tail; lives in large colonies and eats mainly seeds; courts, mates, and has nests several times a year; nests on rock ledges; Columba via; used as food and for sacrifices; regarded as swift, docile, and innocent
s.c: Though in English a relatively clear distinction is made between ‘doves’ (which have pointed tails) and ‘pigeons’ (which have square off tails), there seems to be no such distinction in the use of περιστερά and τρυγών in the Greek of the New Testament.|There are, however, certain problems involved in the connotations of terms relating to pigeons or doves. According to ancient zoology, the dove was thought to have no bile, and consequently, therefore, to be a very peaceful and clean bird. It thus became a symbol of Christian virtue and of gentleness (as in ⟦Matthew 10:16|Matthew 10:16⟧). In reality, however, doves and pigeons are quite aggressive, and a group of pigeons are frequently known to peck an injured bird to death. Therefore, in some societies pigeons or doves are not regarded as gentle or peaceful, but rather as wicked and harmful. In fact, in some cultures doves are thought to be symbols of death and of evil. Under such circumstances it is important, therefore, to have some marginal note so as to indicate clearly the symbolic significance of such birds in biblical contexts.

s.dp: Artifacts › Images and Idols
s.d: an object (not necessarily three-dimensional) which has been formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
s.c: In certain contexts the referents of εἰκών, τύπος, and χάραγμα may have special religious significance in that they may refer to idols, but the focal component for the translator is that of a likeness or resemblance. In contexts such as ⟦Matthew 22:20|Matthew 22:20⟧ an equivalent translation may be simply a picture, but in ⟦Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23⟧ and ⟦Acts 7:43|Acts 7:43⟧ one may use the same expression as is employed to render εἴδωλον idol (LN 6.97).

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a visual form designed to be imitated or copied

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Archetype, Corresponding Type [Antitype]
s.d: a model or example which anticipates or precedes a later realization

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Class, Kind
s.d: a kind or class, implying a relationship to some model or pattern
s.c: For another interpretation of τύπος in ⟦Acts 23:25|Acts 23:25⟧, see LN 90.28.

s.dp: Case › Content
s.d: the content of a discourse or a document
s.c: For another interpretation of τύπος in ⟦Acts 23:25|Acts 23:25⟧, see LN 58.25.

s.dp: Physical Impact › Hit, Strike
s.d: to strike or hit an object, one or more times
s.g: to hit; to strike; to beat
s.c: Note that the imperfect tense may be used of a repeated action, and therefore the translation ‘beat.’ ἔτυπτεν τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ ‘he beat his breast’ ⟦Luke 18:13|Luke 18:13⟧. The action of ‘beating the breast’ in ⟦Luke 18:13|Luke 18:13⟧ is symbolic in that it has the meaning of repentance and contrition. In other languages, however, the expression ‘to beat the breast’ may constitute a symbol of pride or self-flattery. In some languages the equivalent of the biblical expression ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to strike the head’ or ‘to grasp the abdomen.’

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:τύπτω<SDBG:τύπτω:000000>}[a] ‘to strike, to beat,’ {D:19.1}) to cause serious harm to, in a psychological sense

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an Ephesian in whose hall Paul lectured

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Τύρος<SDBG:Τύρος:000000>} ‘Tyre,’ {D:93.602}) a person who lives in or is a native of Tyre

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city on the Phoenician coast

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › See
s.d: pertaining to being unable to see

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:τυφλός<SDBG:τυφλός:000000>}[a] ‘unable to see, blind,’ {D:24.38}) pertaining to not being able to understand
s.g: unable to understand; incapable of comprehending; blind
s.c: In a number of languages it is possible to preserve the figurative meaning of ‘blind’; in certain instances, however, part of the figurative meaning may be retained by translating ‘not able to see how to live’ or ‘not able to see the truth.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (a causative derivative of {L:τυφλός<SDBG:τυφλός:000001>}[b] unable to understand, {D:32.42}) to cause someone not to be able to understand
s.g: to make someone not understand; to remove someone’s understanding

s.dp: Understand › Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to blind the eyes) to cause someone to no longer have the capacity for understanding
s.g: to cause to not understand; to make unable to comprehend
s.c: Though in some languages there is a close relationship between the eyes and comprehension, in many languages it is simply impossible to use the idiom ‘to blind the eyes’ in speaking of ‘causing someone not to understand.’ The problem becomes particularly difficult in speaking of ‘darkness blinding the eyes’ as in ⟦1 John 2:11|1 John 2:11⟧. People can understand how ‘bright light would blind the eyes,’ but it would be strange indeed to think of ‘darkness’ having such an effect. In the context of ⟦1 John 2:11|1 John 2:11⟧, the darkness is, of course, not literal darkness but a state of sinfulness. Therefore, in some languages it may be necessary to translate ‘their sinfulness has made it impossible for them to understand’ or ‘because they sin, they cannot understand.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of τυφόομαι ‘to be crazy, to be demented,’ not occurring in the NT) to be so arrogant as to be practically demented
s.g: to be insanely arrogant; to be extremely proud; to be very arrogant

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Burning
s.d: the process of burning slowly, with accompanying smoke and relatively little glow
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 12:20|Matthew 12:20⟧ the burning of the wick may be described as ‘to burn very slowly’ or ‘to burn just a little,’ but it may be more satisfactory to render τύφομαι in terms of the amount of light which is shown, for example, ‘causing just a little light’ or ‘shining only a little as it burns.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Wind
s.d: (derivative of τυφῶν ‘Typhon,’ the legendary father of the winds, not occurring in the NT) pertaining to a very strong wind
s.c: Expressions for strong winds often differ on the basis of two important features: (1) the strength or violence of the wind and (2) the duration of the wind. For example, in English terms such as squall and tornado indicate violent but short periods of blowing, while hurricane or typhoon indicates a storm which takes a much longer period of time to pass. In ⟦Acts 27:14|Acts 27:14⟧ the reference is obviously to the latter type of storm, called typhoon, hurricane, or monsoon, depending upon the region in which such violent and protracted storms occur.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a leader from the province of Asia who was associated with Paul

s.dp: Features of Objects › Color
s.d: pertaining to being the color of the flower hyacinth (see {D:2.41}), probably a shade of blue
s.c: Since in some languages the flower hyacinth may not be as well known as precious stones such as sapphire and turquoise, it may be possible to render ⟦Revelation 9:17|Revelation 9:17⟧ as ‘blue as sapphire’ or ‘blue as turquoise.’ The justification for this is simply that the Greek term ὑακίνθινος had become primarily a designation for color.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: jacinth or hyacinth, probably blue in color (see {D:2.29})

s.dp: Artifacts › Miscellaneous
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὕαλος<SDBG:ὕαλος:000000>}[a] ‘glass,’ {D:6.222}) consisting of or pertaining to glass

s.dp: Artifacts › Miscellaneous
s.d: a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
s.c: It is also possible that ὕαλος should be interpreted as crystal; see LN 2.46). In ⟦Revelation 21:18|Revelation 21:18⟧ and ⟦Revelation 21:21|Revelation 21:21⟧ the emphasis is upon the transparency of the glass.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
s.c: The equivalent of ‘crystal’ is often a descriptive phrase such as ‘a brilliant stone’ or ‘a shining stone’ or ‘a glass-like stone.’ In developing a satisfactory term for crystal, it is important to avoid possible confusion with diamond.|Some scholars, however, interpret ὕαλος in ⟦Revelation 21:21|Revelation 21:21⟧ as ‘glass’ (see LN 6.222).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Treat Badly
s.d: to maltreat in an insolent manner
s.g: to maltreat; to mistreat with insolence
s.c: In a number of contexts ὑβρίζω seems to combine not only the maltreatment of persons but the attitude of insolence on the part of the one who maltreats another. Therefore, it may be useful in some instances to employ a double expression, for example, ‘to look down upon and to maltreat.’

s.dp: Communication › Insult, Slander
s.d: to speak against someone in an insolent and arrogant way

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Treat Badly
s.d: to be insolently mistreated
s.c: It is also possible to understand ὕβρις in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:10|2 Corinthians 12:10⟧ as actual physical violence (see LN 20.19) or as insults (see LN 33.391).

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: the condition resulting from violence or mistreatment
s.c: It is possible to interpret ὕβρις in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:10|2 Corinthians 12:10⟧ as ‘insults’ (see LN 33.391) or as ‘insolent mistreatment’ (see LN 88.131).

s.dp: Communication › Insult, Slander
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑβρίζω<SDBG:ὑβρίζω:000001>}[b] ‘to insult,’ {D:33.390}) the content of an insulting statement
s.c: In ⟦2 Corinthians 12:10|2 Corinthians 12:10⟧ it is not possible to determine whether ὕβρις refers to the content of the slanderous words or to the event of being slandered. For other interpretations of ὕβρις in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:10|2 Corinthians 12:10⟧, see LN 88.131 and LN 20.19.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Treat Badly
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑβρίζω<SDBG:ὑβρίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to mistreat with insolence,’ {D:88.130}) one who maltreats others with insolence
s.c: It is important to recognize in the term ὑβριστής more than merely an attitude of pride, for ὑβρίζω implies an attitude of superiority which results in mistreatment of and violent acts against others.

s.dp: Communication › Insult, Slander
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑβρίζω<SDBG:ὑβρίζω:000001>}[b] to insult, {D:33.390}) one who insults in an arrogant manner

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: the state of being healthy, well (in contrast with sickness)
s.g: to be well; to be healthy
s.c: In a number of languages health is expressed only in terms of strength, for ‘to be well’ is ‘to be strong.’ In other languages, however, to be well or to be healthy is a negation of illness or sickness, so that in ⟦Mark 16:18|Mark 16:18⟧ one may translate ‘they will place their hands on those who are sick and these people will become not sick.’

s.dp: True, False › Accurate, Inaccurate
s.d: (derivative of {L:ὑγιής<SDBG:ὑγιής:000001>}[b] ‘right, accurate,’ {D:72.14}) to be correct in one’s views, with the implication of such a state being positively valued
s.g: to be correct; to be sound; to be accurate

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Health, Vigor, Strength
s.d: the state of being healthy, well (in contrast with sickness)
s.g: to be well; to be healthy
s.c: In a number of languages health is expressed only in terms of strength, for ‘to be well’ is ‘to be strong.’ In other languages, however, to be well or to be healthy is a negation of illness or sickness, so that in ⟦Mark 16:18|Mark 16:18⟧ one may translate ‘they will place their hands on those who are sick and these people will become not sick.’

s.dp: True, False › Accurate, Inaccurate
s.d: pertaining to being accurate, as well as useful and beneficial
